description: How a package signature is produced and what bytes a verifier must check. Written so that a Go, a Rust and a JavaScript verifier accept and reject exactly the same inputs.
status_of_this_contract: The v1 section below describes what NilLang's pkg/signing actually does and is enforced against NilLang's own tooling. It is NOT yet what every verifier in the ecosystem does: see known_divergences, which is the single most important thing in this file until it is resolved.

known_divergences.what: The store signs the raw package bytes directly with Ed25519 and stores the signature base64-encoded, with the key named by a friendly identifier such as "onuron-team" in trusted-keys.json.
known_divergences.contract_says: NilLang signs a JSON payload {"checksum","timestamp","key_id"} with the signature in lowercase hex and the key id derived from SHA-256 over the public key.
known_divergences.why_it_matters: These are two signature schemes over the same artifact. A package signed for the store cannot be verified by a device using the NilLang verifier, and vice versa. Every claim of "one signature chain" is currently false.
known_divergences.cannot_be_fixed_by_editing_the_contract: Six packages are published under the store scheme. Declaring the store scheme canonical would require re-signing all of them with a key this repository does not hold.
options: Adopt the store scheme ecosystem-wide and deprecate NilLang's SigningPayload. Simplest; discards the timestamp binding, which is the one property the NilLang payload has that the store scheme lacks.
Adopt the NilLang payload ecosystem-wide and re-sign the six published packages. Preserves the timestamp binding; requires the maintainer's signing key and a coordinated release.

Carry both: the contract defines two named schemes and a verifier is told which one a package uses. Honest, and it preserves every existing package — at the cost of a permanent branch in every verifier.
known_divergences.blocks: Contract G's goal that Go, Rust and JavaScript accept and reject the same inputs
known_divergences.interim_rule: Until this is resolved, no verifier may claim to verify "the" Onuron signature. A verifier states which scheme it implements. This file implements package_signature_v1; the store implements store-signing-raw-bytes.

why_this_is_specified: Five verifiers will read this: the NilLang CLI, OnuronOS at install time, the emulator in CI, the Onuron Project store API, and any third-party package manager. A signature scheme with two valid encodings of the same payload is a signature scheme with no signature. Everything below is stated as bytes, not as 'the JSON'.

algorithms.signature_encoding: lowercase hex, no 0x prefix, exactly 128 characters
algorithms.note: Ed25519 hashes internally. The SHA-256 below is the package digest, not a pre-hash fed to the signature.

algorithms.signature_encoding: base64, exactly 88 characters decoding to 64 bytes
algorithms.public_key_encoding: base64, decoding to a raw 32-byte key
algorithms.digest: none — the raw package bytes are the signed message
algorithms.note: The scheme the Onuron Project store uses today. See known_divergences. It is listed here so that a verifier can identify it rather than misparse it as package_signature_v1.

unknown_algorithm: refuse. A verifier must not skip a signature it does not recognise.

key_id.derivation: lowercase hex of the first 16 bytes of SHA-256 over the 32-byte public key
key_id.why: A key id that a verifier cannot recompute from the key it holds is an identifier, not a binding. Recomputing it is how a verifier refuses a key id that was swapped onto a different key.

fingerprint.derivation: first 20 bytes of SHA-256 over the public key, hex, grouped into 4-character groups separated by ':'
fingerprint.purpose: human comparison only; never used in a verification decision

record.note: A key with purpose 'encryption' presented as a signing key is refused. The field exists; nothing enforces it yet.

signed_payload.description: Three fields, serialised as compact JSON with no whitespace, in exactly this order. The order is the struct field order in pkg/signing; it is fixed here because a verifier reconstructs the payload rather than reading it from the file.

fields_in_order.name: checksum
fields_in_order.encoding: lowercase hex, 64 characters, SHA-256 over the entire .nilax file

signed_payload.why_excluded: signed_at is wall-clock time of the signing operation and can differ from the signed timestamp. Including it means a signature that verifies at signing time fails to verify on read, and the natural fix — the one every implementer reaches for — is to trust the file's own signed_at. Excluding it means a file that disagrees with its signature is simply wrong.

verification_order.action: look the key id up in the trust store
check the key is not revoked and is within its validity window
recompute the key id from the stored public key and compare
recompute SHA-256 over the file and compare with checksum
rebuild the canonical payload bytes and verify the Ed25519 signature

package_signature_v1.ordering_rule: Integrity is checked before the signature. A verifier that runs the signature first spends attacker-controlled time on data it is about to discard.

manifest_signature_v2.description: v2 signs the manifest itself rather than the container, so a verifier can check what the package claims before it unpacks anything.

canonicalisation.rule: serialise the manifest as JSON with object keys sorted lexicographically by UTF-8 code unit, no insignificant whitespace, UTF-8, and the `signature` member removed before signing
canonicalisation.why: Three implementations parsing the same JSON object into three maps produce three byte strings unless the encoding is pinned. Sorting and stripping is the smallest rule that removes the difference.

signed_fields.rule: The signature covers exactly the members listed in `signature.signed_fields`, and the list is stored in the signature so that adding a manifest field is a visible act rather than an accident.
signed_fields.why_metadata_is_excluded: Metadata is presentation. Signing it would force a re-signature every time a description is corrected, and a re-signature is an operational event people avoid, so signing it would push people toward not signing at all.

certificate_signature.description: pkg/signing also implements an X.509-shaped certificate chain on the same Ed25519 primitive. It is not part of the package trust path.
gaps: No trust root is published. VerifyChain takes a root public key as an argument, so trust is whatever the caller supplies.
Chain construction is not verified on the verifier side beyond pairwise signatures; issuer/subject linkage is not checked.
Nothing in the package path consults a certificate.
certificate_signature.consequence: Do not present the certificate chain as a second trust mechanism. It is a library that has not been connected.

private_keys.must: live only in an approved signing environment or a build secret store
must_not: appear in a website asset, a build artifact, or a public log
be the same key as the one used for development or CI experiments

public_keys.rule: revocation and trust provenance live beside it as a separate, dated document, so that adding a key and justifying it are two different acts

rotation.rule: A release signed by a key retired after that release keeps verifying. Key id, signature and package digest are recorded per release so a rotation does not invalidate history.
rotation.pending: The rotation and revocation process is written here but not yet exercised by a tool. Until it is, treat `revoked` in a key record as documentation.

release_record.rule: An official release records: source revision, compiler revision, package digest, signature key id, emulator test evidence, and store API version. A release missing any of these is not publishable.
release_record.owner: onuron_project publishes the record; nilLang supplies the compiler revision and package digest.

cross_language_verification.test_vectors: contracts/testdata/signing/v1-vectors.json holds signed payloads with their canonical bytes, so a Rust or JavaScript verifier can be checked against Go without a live key.
cross_language_verification.conformance_gate: Every verifier in the ecosystem runs the same vectors and must produce identical accept/reject decisions. A vector that one implementation treats differently is a contract bug, not an implementation bug, until proven otherwise.
